Editorial framing AI-drafted, status:draft, pending Wilson's curation. [v2 migration 2026-09-10: gravity/synthesis moved under tracks.semicontinuous (verified against that track's first reading, not assumed); the other track has firstReading only, pending Phase 4b authoring.] [Phase 4b 2026-09-10, Opus: Gospel doors gained Wesley (18:15) and Glossa (Migne 18:15) witnesses; complementary half authored — gravity, synthesis, two Ezekiel 33 doors. Ezekiel is not in Migne's Glossa and Wesley has one note on these verses, so the first-reading doors lean on Catena's intertextual notes (how the NT takes up the watchman and the oath of 33:11), which are retrieved text rows, not recall.]
trap: Becomes a weapon (church discipline as public shaming, or a rulebook for cutting someone off) or is avoided altogether ("just forgive and forget," skip the confrontation) — missing that the goal named at each step is to *gain* the brother, not to win an argument.
hinge: The process ends in a possible verdict of "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector" — yet Jesus spent his whole ministry eating with Gentiles and tax collectors. The most severe thing this text allows is: treat him like someone I would still go find.

doors.claim: Confrontation begins one-on-one, in private, because shame compounds sin rather than curing it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Thy brother is to be reproved in private, lest if once he has lost a sense of shame, he should continue in sin.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Our Lord admonishes us not to overlook one another's faults, yet not so as seeking for matter of blame, but watching what you may amend.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Go and reprove him alone — if it may be in person; if that cannot so well be done, by thy messenger; or in writing. Observe, our Lord gives no liberty to omit this; or to exchange it for either of the following steps.

doors.say: The first move is never public — not because sin should be hidden, but because shame, once a person loses it, stops correcting anything.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they're tempted to expose rather than approach, and go to that person alone first.

doors.claim: Reconciliation is a gain for both people, not a victory for one — the goal reframes confrontation as rescue, not conquest.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He said not, he has gained himself, but, you have gained him; which shews that both of you are the gainers.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: For in saving another, salvation is gained for ourselves also.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: We ought to rebuke the sinner with a zeal for justice, and open the bowels of mercy to him that repents. He sins thus, who seeing his brother sin keeps silent.

doors.say: When you go to confront someone, you're not just trying to fix them — you're trying to get both of you back.
doors.do: Have them reframe one grievance they're holding as a potential mutual gain, not a case to win.

doors.landing: Like a Gentile and a tax collector
doors.claim: The harshest verdict this text allows is to treat someone the way Jesus treated Gentiles and tax collectors — which is to say, still pursued, still eaten with, never written off.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: That He says, 'As a heathen and a publican,' shews that he is to be more abhorred, who under the name of a believer does the deeds of an unbeliever.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Though even thus we are not to neglect his salvation; for the heathens themselves, that is, the gentiles...

doors.say: Even the worst verdict in this text isn't exile — it's the status Jesus spent his whole ministry crossing over to reach.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they've functionally written off, and identify one way Jesus would still be pursuing that person.

doors.claim: The watchman is responsible for sounding the warning, not for whether it is heeded; Scripture takes that charge up again in the apostles.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The watchman who warns the wicked and is not heeded 'has delivered his soul' — exactly Paul's claim 'I am clean' (taken up at Acts 18:5-6).

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The watchman who warns the wicked to turn 'will have saved his life' is the prophetic logic behind saving a soul from death by turning the sinner back (taken up at James 5:13-18).

doors.say: You are not responsible for how someone answers the truth. You are responsible for telling it.
doors.do: Ask them to name the warning they have been holding back from someone they love, and to speak it this week, gently and alone.

doors.landing: No pleasure in the death of the wicked
doors.claim: To people who say it is too late for them, God swears by his own life that he wants them to turn and live.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Our sins — the unpardoned guilt, and the unsupportable punishment of our sins; we shall pine away, 'tis too late to hope. How can it be better with us?

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The oath 'As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live' restates the divine saving desire (taken up at 1 Timothy 2:1-7).

doors.say: They said it was too late. God answered with an oath: I want you to live.
doors.do: Invite anyone who has decided they are beyond turning to hear this oath as addressed to them, and to take one step back toward God.

complementary.gravity: God makes Ezekiel a watchman who must warn the wicked or answer for their blood, and swears, "As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33); the Psalm asks to be taught the way of God's statutes; Paul says love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13); and Jesus lays out how to go to a brother who has sinned. The nerve: love that speaks the hard word, because God wants the sinner to live.

synthesis.convergence: The watchman who stays silent shares the guilt, and God pleads for the wicked to turn and live (Ezekiel 33); the psalmist asks to be turned from vanity toward God's way (Psalm 119); Paul sums every command in the debt of love (Romans 13); and Jesus sends us first, alone, to the one who wronged us (Matthew 18). Each reading makes honest warning a form of love, and aims it at life rather than punishment.
synthesis.claim: Silence is not kindness when someone is heading toward harm: love speaks, because God wants them to live.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that avoids conflict by avoiding truth, the move is to recover the watchman's word as care — spoken privately, first, and for the other person's life rather than our own vindication.

semicontinuous.gravity: Israel marks the Passover with blood on the doorposts, the sign that turns death aside (Exodus 12); Paul reduces the whole law to one debt that's never paid off — "owe no one anything, except to love one another" (Romans 13); and Jesus gives a specific procedure for confronting sin in the community — private first, then witnesses, then the whole church. The nerve: love for the offender, not exposure of the offender, drives every step of the process.

synthesis.convergence: Passover blood marks a door so death passes over, not so the household is exposed (Exodus 12); Paul reduces every commandment to one unpaid debt — love (Romans 13); and Jesus' whole procedure for confronting sin aims at gathering back in, ending in the promise that where two or three gather in his name, he is there. Every reading refuses a religion of exposure for a religion of restoration.
synthesis.claim: The point of naming what's wrong is never exposure — it's the door left open for someone to come back through.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that either weaponizes accountability or avoids it entirely, name the actual goal Jesus gives: not being right, not being safe from confrontation, but gaining each other back.

subtract: Three landings — the private first step, the mutual gain, or what the harshest verdict actually permits. Choose one and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), and Catena's intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
